periods.activity_title: Who Does What? Reading Anu and Kabir's World
periods.section_anchor: Opening narrative (Anu, Kabir and the people in their lives)
materials: Individual activity sheets with a two-column table (Person / Activity described)

time_bands.activity: Students read the opening narrative silently — Anu and Kabir observe a neighbour who is an IAF pilot earning a salary, a retired BSF officer who voluntarily teaches geography and gardens, parents running a garment shop, a mother who volunteers with a community knitting group, and an elder brother who engineers software and also volunteers to teach computing on weekends. After reading, each student fills column 1 of their activity sheet by listing every person named and one-line description of what that person does.

Students attempt the Let's Explore task: they examine their completed list and place each activity into one of two provisional columns — 'seems connected to earning money' or 'does not seem connected to earning money.' They work individually first, then compare with a partner, noting any disagreements and writing one sentence explaining why a particular activity was hard to place.

The class examines three contested cases whole-group: the retired BSF officer teaching geography (no pay, but a former paid career), the mother knitting with the community group (no pay, social benefit), and the brother volunteering computing skills (no pay, alongside a paid job). For each, the teacher asks: 'What is the person getting out of this activity — money, something else, or nothing at all?' Students revise their classifications on their sheets, writing a reason beside each changed entry.

Students write two sentences in their notebooks: one stating the question the narrative raises ('What makes an activity economic or non-economic?') and one describing the activity in the narrative they found hardest to classify and why. These become the students' own inquiry anchor for the chapter's central question.

periods.section_context: IAF pilot, BSF volunteer teacher, garment shop parents, knitting group, software volunteer
periods.teacher_notes: The opening narrative deliberately places paid and unpaid activities side by side without labelling them, inviting students to notice the distinction before the chapter names it. A common confusion here is treating 'important' as a synonym for 'economic' — students may assume the volunteer teacher is doing economic work because teaching matters greatly; draw out that significance and monetary exchange are separate questions.

periods.activity_title: Naming the Exchange: Forms of Payment in Economic Activities
materials: Vocabulary card set (one card each: money's worth, market, fee, salary, wage, payment in kind) — students create these from their notebooks in the opening band

time_bands.activity: Students read the vocabulary definitions in the textbook — money's worth, market, fee, salary, wage, payment in kind — and create a small reference card for each term in their notebooks: term on top, definition in their own words below. The teacher circulates and checks that 'payment in kind' is distinguished from barter (the chapter does not use that word; keep to the chapter's own framing).

Students read the Kavya narrative: her uncle earns a monthly salary as a construction-company technician; her aunt earns a salary at the post office and a weekly fee for online classes; farm labourer Sahil earns a daily wage partly in cash and partly in mangoes (payment in kind). Students annotate each person in the narrative by writing the correct payment term from their cards beside the person's name, then answer: 'Why does Sahil's payment in mangoes count as economic — what exactly is being exchanged?'

Each pair creates a two-column matching exercise — left column: five brief scenario descriptions drawn from the chapter's examples (business person selling school bags, lawyer arguing a case, truck driver transporting goods, factory workers, Sahil the farm labourer); right column: the payment form. Pairs exchange sheets with another pair and complete each other's matching task, then return and discuss any disagreements, citing the chapter definition to resolve them.

The teacher poses the Think About It prompt from the textbook: 'Recall two economic activities you observed on your way to school and identify how those workers were likely paid.' Students write their answers individually. Two or three students share, and the class confirms whether each activity and payment form fits the chapter's definitions.

periods.section_context: Salary, fee, wage, payment in kind; Kavya's uncle, aunt, Sahil in Kamlapur
periods.teacher_notes: Having encountered paid and unpaid activities in the opening narrative, students now build precise vocabulary for the monetary side of the distinction. The most frequent confusion is between wage and salary — students tend to use them interchangeably; anchor the difference in the chapter's own phrasing ('fixed regular payment monthly' vs 'payment for a specific period of time'). The Sahil mango example is the chapter's sharpest test of understanding payment in kind; if students say mangoes are not money, ask them whether Sahil received something of economic value — the chapter's definition of money's worth resolves it.

competency_edges.competency_text: Identify key elements of economic activities, forms of compensation, and value addition in production and exchange.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can classify forms of compensation by applying definitional criteria to real worker scenarios.

periods.activity_title: Adding Value: How Work Transforms Raw Materials
materials: Blackboard or chart paper for a class value-addition chain
periods.visual_aids: A simple three-box flow drawn on the blackboard: [Raw Wood ₹600] → [Rajesh's Skill, Time, Effort] → [Finished Chair ₹1,000]

time_bands.activity: The teacher draws the three-box flow on the blackboard and asks students to read the Rajesh-the-carpenter paragraph in the textbook. Students identify the input cost (₹600 for wood), the output price (₹1,000 for the chair), and calculate the difference (₹400). The teacher asks: 'What does the ₹400 represent — where did it come from?' Students write one sentence answering before sharing.

Students work on the Let's Explore activity from the textbook: they examine a list of professions and activities and assess which ones create monetary value and which do not, writing one reason per item. They then add two examples of their own — one from their immediate experience and one they invent — explaining what the input is, what the output is, and what has been added.

Small groups of three build a value-addition chain for one of their own examples on a strip of paper: they draw the same three-box model (input → transformation → output) and annotate the middle box with what the worker contributes (skill, time, effort, knowledge). Groups post their strips on the board and do a gallery read, placing a tick beside chains they find convincing and a question mark beside any they find unclear, with a brief note explaining the question.

The class addresses the question marks: for each queried chain, the group that made it defends or revises it using the chapter's definition — 'economic activities add value at each stage of transforming something from one form into another.' The teacher closes by asking: 'Is every transformation an economic activity, or does the definition require something more?' Students write a one-sentence answer.

periods.section_context: Rajesh the carpenter, wood-to-chair value addition, ₹600 input and ₹1,000 output
periods.teacher_notes: Having classified payment forms in the previous unit, students now examine what gives economic activities their monetary value — the process of transformation. A common confusion is treating value addition as simply 'profit'; the chapter's framing is broader — the ₹400 represents skill, time, and effort, not only markup. When students build their own chains, the middle box is the most important: if it names only 'work' without specifying what the worker contributes, prompt them to name the specific skill or knowledge involved.

competency_edges.competency_text: Identify key elements of economic activities, forms of compensation, and value addition in production and exchange.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can construct a value-addition sequence that traces how a worker's skill and effort transform inputs into outputs of greater economic worth.

materials: Scenario cards (teacher-prepared, one per pair): brief descriptions of six activities mixing economic and non-economic

time_bands.activity: Students read the non-economic activities section in the textbook. They identify the four motivations the chapter names — gratitude, love, care, respect — and the examples given: parents cooking for the family, helping children with schoolwork, youth caring for grandparents, family members assisting with home renovation. Students write a one-sentence summary of what distinguishes a non-economic activity from an economic one, using only the chapter's definition.

Pairs receive a scenario card with six brief activity descriptions (e.g., 'A doctor treats a patient for a fee,' 'A daughter helps her father prepare for a presentation,' 'A shopkeeper sells vegetables,' 'A neighbour teaches a child to ride a bicycle,' 'A factory worker assembles phones on a production line,' 'A grandmother knits a sweater for her grandchild'). For each scenario, the pair writes: economic or non-economic, and the specific reason from the chapter's definition.

Pairs join into groups of four and compare their classifications. Where they disagree, they must identify which word in the chapter's definition is being read differently. Each group picks their single hardest case and writes a one-paragraph argument for their classification, quoting the chapter's definition to justify it.

Each group reads their hardest case and argument aloud. The class votes — economic or non-economic — and the teacher facilitates resolution by returning always to the chapter's language: 'Does it involve money or is it performed in exchange for money or money's worth?' Students note the final agreed classification and the key phrase from the definition that settled the debate.

periods.section_context: Parents cooking, helping with schoolwork, caring for grandparents, home renovation as non-economic
periods.teacher_notes: The chapter insists that non-economic activities are not lesser in importance than economic ones — only different in whether money changes hands. A predictable confusion is that 'important' activities must be economic; the grandparent-care and cooking examples exist precisely to show high social value without monetary exchange. The scenario-card debate is most productive when students quote the exact definition rather than arguing from intuition — redirect any intuition-based claim to the chapter's specific wording.

competency_edges.competency_text: Identify key elements of economic activities, forms of compensation, and value addition in production and exchange.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can distinguish economic from non-economic activities by applying the chapter's definitional criteria to unfamiliar scenarios.

periods.activity_title: Sevā in Practice: Selfless Service as a Non-Economic Form

time_bands.activity: Students read the sevā section in the textbook. They identify two institutional examples — langars at gurudwaras (food served freely to every visitor) and distribution of prasād at temples — and write in their notebooks what each example has in common: no payment is sought or received, the service is open to everyone, and the motivation is contribution to society without expectation of return.

Students respond to the Think About It prompt from the textbook: compare Kabir's grandfather voluntarily teaching neighbourhood children with a paid school teacher. They write a structured comparison with three labelled rows — What the person does, How they are compensated, What motivates them — and then add a fourth row of their own: What the community gains from each. Students do this individually before sharing with a partner.

Students write a short reflective piece (one substantial paragraph) responding to this question: 'The chapter says sevā fosters a sense of satisfaction and gratitude. What does it mean to gain satisfaction from an activity that has no monetary reward? Describe one non-economic activity that is meaningful in your own family and explain what value it creates for the people involved.' The chapter's framing of 'contributing to society without expecting anything in return' must appear somewhere in their writing.

Three or four students read their reflections aloud. After each reading, the class identifies which aspect of the chapter's definition of sevā the student's example best illustrates — selflessness, openness to all, or satisfaction from contribution. The teacher notes on the board which aspects appear most and least often across the examples shared, and asks: 'Does every non-economic activity count as sevā, or does the chapter reserve that word for something specific?'

periods.section_context: Langars at gurudwaras, prasād at temples, Kabir's grandfather teaching voluntarily
periods.teacher_notes: The sevā section draws on India's tradition of communal giving across religious institutions — gurudwaras and temples — to illustrate that selfless service is a structured social practice, not an accident. A common confusion is treating sevā as identical to any non-economic activity; the chapter implies sevā has a specific character — it is outward-facing, community-serving, and entirely without expectation of return — so the closing question about whether every non-economic activity qualifies is worth pressing. Students' reflections will often name family examples that are deeply meaningful but inward-facing (a grandmother's cooking for family), which is a useful contrast for drawing the boundary.

competency_edges.competency_text: Appreciate India's tradition of selfless communal giving and distinguish it from paid activity.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain how institutional sevā practices embody the principle of selfless service and differ from compensated work.

periods.activity_title: Collective Action: Community Programmes and Their Social Significance
periods.visual_aids: Two-column table on the blackboard: Programme Name | What the community does together | What the collective effect is

time_bands.activity: Students read the community participation section in the textbook. They identify the two named examples — Swachh Bharat Abhiyan (citizens maintaining personal spaces and cleaning streets, parks, and public areas collectively) and Van Mahotsav (community tree-plantation drives promoting forest conservation awareness) — and note for each: what individuals do, what the group does together, and what the collective outcome is.

Students respond to the Think About It prompt: they identify similar community practices from their own area, reflect on whether festival celebrations constitute non-economic activities, and describe community programmes undertaken by their school or locality. Each student writes three entries in their notebook — one for a community cleaning or environmental practice, one for a festival, one for a school or locality programme — answering for each: Is this non-economic? What makes it non-economic or not?

The class builds a shared table on the blackboard: students contribute their three entries by naming programme, collective action taken, and collective outcome. As entries accumulate, the teacher asks: 'What do Swachh Bharat Abhiyan and Van Mahotsav have in common that makes community participation stronger than individual action alone?' Students analyse the table and write a one-sentence answer using evidence from at least two programmes named on the board.

Students write a final analytical sentence in their notebooks: 'Community participation adds value to non-economic activities because…' followed by a specific example from either the textbook or the class-assembled table. The teacher collects two or three examples and reads them aloud, asking the class to confirm whether the reasoning holds against the chapter's own evidence.

periods.section_context: Swachh Bharat Abhiyan, Van Mahotsav, community cleaning and tree-plantation drives
periods.teacher_notes: The chapter distinguishes individual non-economic action from organised community participation — Swachh Bharat Abhiyan works because it combines personal maintenance with collective street and park cleaning to produce a neighbourhood-scale outcome neither could achieve alone. A predictable confusion is whether festival celebrations are non-economic; the chapter does not resolve this directly, so treat it as a genuine inquiry question: do participants expect monetary compensation, or is the motivation social and cultural? When students build the class table, push them to state the collective effect specifically — 'clean streets' is weaker than 'a neighbourhood where residents and visitors can move and gather without health hazard.'

competency_edges.competency_text: Collect information about organised social institutions and practices in one's vicinity and interpret their significance for human society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can interpret how organised community programmes achieve outcomes for human society that individual action alone cannot.

periods.activity_title: The Full Picture: Economic, Non-Economic, and Community Value Together
periods.section_anchor: Types of Economic Activities / The Importance of Non-Economic Activities / Sevā: selfless service / The strength of community participation
materials: A set of six activity cards per pair (teacher-prepared): two clearly economic, two clearly non-economic including one sevā example, one community programme example

time_bands.activity: Pairs receive six activity cards. They sort the cards into three labelled columns: Economic Activity, Non-Economic Activity (personal/family), and Non-Economic Activity (community/sevā). For each card, they write the key criterion from the chapter that placed it in that column — the sorting itself forces them to distinguish between the three categories the chapter has built.

Each pair selects one card from the economic column and one from the non-economic column and writes a structured comparison: What does the activity produce or contribute? Who benefits and how? What is the motivation of the person doing it? What would be lost if no one did it? Both comparisons must use vocabulary from the chapter — salary, wage, fee, payment in kind, money's worth, value addition, sevā — wherever appropriate.

Pairs join into groups of four and share their comparisons. The group identifies one insight that surprised them — a place where their comparison revealed something about economic or non-economic activities they had not noticed before — and writes it as a single precise sentence: 'We discovered that… because the chapter shows that…' Two groups share their insight sentences with the whole class.

Students individually write a closing analytical statement answering the chapter's central question: 'The chapter is called The Value of Work — what kinds of value does it say work can have?' Their answer must name at least three distinct kinds of value the chapter discusses (monetary, social, communal, personal) and support each with a specific example from the chapter.

periods.section_context: Economic activities, non-economic activities, sevā, community participation synthesised through chapter vocabulary
periods.teacher_notes: This unit draws together the distinctions the chapter has built — economic activities and their forms of payment, non-economic activities and their social importance, sevā as a structured communal tradition, and community participation as a force multiplier for non-economic work. A common confusion at this stage is collapsing sevā and community participation into a single category; the chapter keeps them distinct — sevā has an institutional and spiritual register, while community programmes like Swachh Bharat Abhiyan operate at a civic and governmental scale. The closing analytical statement is the most demanding move of the unit: circulate during writing and check that students are naming distinct kinds of value, not restating the same idea with different words.

competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can analyse the chapter's full range of activities to distinguish the defining features of economic activities across forms of compensation and value addition.

competency_edges.competency_text: Collect information about organised social institutions and practices in one's vicinity and interpret their significance for human society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain the social significance of community participation programmes by connecting their collective actions to outcomes for human society.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can classify forms of compensation by applying definitional criteria to real worker scenarios.
assessment_items.question_text: Sahil tills land using a tractor. At the end of the day he receives ₹300 in cash and a basket of mangoes as the remainder of his payment. Which term from the chapter best describes the mangoes portion of his payment?

options.label: A
options.text: Fee

options.label: B
options.text: Money's worth as a bonus

options.label: C
options.text: Payment in kind

options.label: D
options.text: Salary

assessment_items.inclusivity: Accept oral responses; allow students to point to the term in their textbook if reading is a barrier.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Confuses salary (fixed monthly payment from an employer) with daily agricultural payment; suggests the student has not distinguished the regularity and employer-employee context of salary.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses fee (payment for professional advice or services) with agricultural wage; indicates the student is applying a professional-services frame to a manual-labour context.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Partially correct — money's worth is a relevant concept — but 'bonus' is not the chapter's term, and applying it here shows the student has grasped the monetary-value idea but has not applied the specific payment-in-kind definition.

assessment_items.chapter_section: Types of Economic Activities / The Importance of Non-Economic Activities / Sevā: selfless service / The strength of community participation
assessment_items.task: Think about the people Anu and Kabir observe — the IAF pilot, the retired BSF officer who teaches geography, the parents running the garment shop, the mother who volunteers with the knitting group, and the brother who volunteers computing skills. Create a comparison table that analyses all five people across four columns: (1) Activity they perform, (2) Economic or Non-Economic — and the reason using the chapter's definition, (3) Form of compensation if economic, or what motivates them if non-economic, (4) What value their activity creates for others or for society. After completing your table, write two sentences below it answering this question: What does the chapter suggest about whether economic activities are more valuable than non-economic ones?
assessment_items.scaffold:
Column 1 — Activity: Describe in one phrase what the person does (e.g., 'serves as a pilot in the Air Force').
Column 2 — Category and Reason: Write 'Economic' or 'Non-Economic' and copy the key phrase from the chapter's definition that places it there.
Column 3 — Compensation or Motivation: For economic activities, name the type of payment (salary / wage / fee / payment in kind). For non-economic activities, name the feeling or value that motivates it (e.g., gratitude, care, service to society).
Column 4 — Value Created: State who benefits and how — this could be financial value, social wellbeing, community benefit, or personal satisfaction.
After the table: In your two sentences, do not simply list examples — make a claim about what the chapter says, then support it with evidence from your table.
format_of_output: A completed five-row comparison table with four labelled columns
Two analytical sentences responding to the closing question
assessment_items.inclusivity: Students who find table construction difficult may use a list format with the four column headers as labels for each person. The teacher may scribe the table structure for students with motor difficulties.

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Students analyse the chapter's full set of opening-narrative characters by applying the economic/non-economic distinction, compensation vocabulary, and value-creation reasoning simultaneously — demonstrating that they can hold multiple analytical dimensions in a single structured task.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: Column 2 is the analytical core: a student who copies a definition without reasoning has met the form but not the substance. Column 3 distinguishes compensation vocabulary (salary, wage, fee, payment in kind) from motivational language (gratitude, care) — a student who writes 'because he likes it' for an economic activity has not applied the chapter's framework. Column 4 pushes beyond classification toward evaluation of social significance. The two closing sentences are the integrative move: look for a claim that engages with the chapter's position on value, not merely a restatement of definitions.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: Column 2 quotes or closely paraphrases the chapter's definition for each entry; Column 3 uses specific payment terms and distinguishes them accurately; Column 4 articulates distinct kinds of value (monetary, social, communal, personal); the two sentences make a defensible claim supported by at least two table entries. Weak: Column 2 uses intuitive labels without definition; Column 3 conflates salary and wage or omits compensation type; Column 4 repeats 'it helps people' without specifying how; the closing sentences restate rather than argue.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The comparison table is the most natural demonstration vehicle for this LO because the task requires students to hold four analytical dimensions simultaneously across five cases — a prose response would collapse the comparisons into narrative; a table preserves the parallel structure that makes the analysis visible and assessable. The teacher may substitute any other format from the assessment menu if it better suits the class.

competency.competency_text: Collect information about organised social institutions and practices in one's vicinity and interpret their significance for human society.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can interpret how organised community programmes achieve outcomes for human society that individual action alone cannot.
assessment_items.question_text: The chapter describes Swachh Bharat Abhiyan as a community-wide non-economic activity. Which of the following best explains why collective participation in this programme achieves something that individual household cleaning alone cannot?

options.label: A
options.text: Community programmes are always organised by the government, which provides resources that individuals lack.

options.label: B
options.text: Individual cleaning is an economic activity, so it does not contribute to community welfare.

options.label: C
options.text: Swachh Bharat Abhiyan succeeds because participants receive payment in kind for their contribution.

options.label: D

what_each_option_reveals.B: Misapplies the economic/non-economic distinction to individual cleaning, suggesting the student conflates the category of an activity with its social worth; also contradicts the chapter's position that individual non-economic action does contribute to welfare.

competency.competency_text: Collect information about organised social institutions and practices in one's vicinity and interpret their significance for human society.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain the social significance of community participation programmes by connecting their collective actions to outcomes for human society.
assessment_items.question_text: Van Mahotsav is described in the chapter as a community participation initiative. Which statement best evaluates its significance for human society?

options.label: A
options.text: It brings community members together for tree plantation drives, promoting awareness of the value of trees and contributing to forest conservation — creating environmental and social benefit beyond what any single household could produce.

options.label: B
options.text: It is significant because it is a religious practice similar to sevā, offering participants spiritual satisfaction.

options.label: C
options.text: It is significant mainly because participants earn wages for planting trees, making it an economic activity that supports livelihoods.

options.label: D
options.text: Its significance lies in being a government festival that replaces individual environmental responsibility with collective government action.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Misclassifies Van Mahotsav as an economic activity by introducing wages, which the chapter does not mention; suggests the student defaults to economic framing when assessing the significance of organised activities.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Introduces a government-replaces-individual framing not in the chapter, and contradicts the chapter's community-participation emphasis; indicates the student may be conflating civic programmes with government-run replacements for individual action.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Conflates Van Mahotsav with sevā by applying a religious-practice frame; suggests the student has not distinguished the chapter's civic community-participation examples from its institutional sevā examples.

competency.competency_text: Collect information about organised social institutions and practices in one's vicinity and interpret their significance for human society.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can interpret how organised community programmes achieve outcomes for human society that individual action alone cannot.
assessment_items.question_text: Using Swachh Bharat Abhiyan as your example, explain in 3–4 sentences how the chapter shows that organised community participation achieves a social outcome that individual action alone cannot. Name the specific collective action the programme involves and the outcome it produces.
expected_elements: Names Swachh Bharat Abhiyan and describes both its individual dimension (maintaining one's own home and surroundings) and its collective dimension (cleaning streets, roads, parks, and public spaces together).
Identifies the collective outcome — a clean neighbourhood and nation — as something that extends beyond what any single household's cleaning could produce.
Explains the logical connection: the outcome is achieved because many individuals act together on shared public spaces, not just on their own private spaces.
assessment_items.inclusivity: Students may use a simple two-row table (Individual action / Collective action) to structure their answer if prose is difficult.

competency.competency_text: Appreciate India's tradition of selfless communal giving and distinguish it from paid activity.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain how institutional sevā practices embody the principle of selfless service and differ from compensated work.
assessment_items.question_text: The chapter describes the practice of langars at gurudwaras as an example of sevā. Which statement best explains what makes this a sevā practice rather than an economic activity?

options.label: A
options.text: It is sevā because food is served freely to every visitor without any expectation of payment or return — the motivation is contribution to society, not monetary exchange.

options.label: B
options.text: It is sevā because the food served at a langar is of lower quality than food sold in markets, so it has no money's worth.

options.label: C
options.text: It is sevā because the gurudwara charges a fee to cover the cost of ingredients, which is a form of payment in kind.

options.label: D
options.text: It is sevā only when performed by paid employees of the gurudwara who donate their salary back to the institution.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Introduces a quality-of-goods argument not present in the chapter — suggests the student is trying to remove economic status by denying money's worth, rather than applying the chapter's no-expectation-of-return criterion.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Misapplies 'fee' and 'payment in kind' — both economic-activity concepts — to a non-economic institutional practice; indicates the student is applying compensation vocabulary from the economic section without distinguishing the sevā context.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Introduces a salary-donation mechanism not in the chapter, and misidentifies who performs sevā; suggests the student is associating sevā with paid workers rather than with the institutional practice of free communal service.

competency.competency_text: Appreciate India's tradition of selfless communal giving and distinguish it from paid activity.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain how institutional sevā practices embody the principle of selfless service and differ from compensated work.
assessment_items.question_text: Kabir's grandfather voluntarily teaches geography to neighbourhood children without any payment. The chapter uses this example alongside langars and prasād distribution to illustrate sevā. What does the chapter identify as the key shared feature that makes all these examples sevā?

options.label: A
options.text: All are performed only by retired or elderly people who no longer need income.

options.label: B
options.text: All are performed within religious institutions, making them spiritual rather than social acts.

options.label: C
options.text: All involve activities that were once paid and have since become voluntary.

options.label: D
options.text: All involve contributing to society without expecting anything in return, fostering satisfaction and gratitude.

assessment_items.inclusivity: Read options aloud for students who need auditory support.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Introduces a 'formerly paid' narrative not present in the chapter — suggests the student is trying to create an economic history for sevā activities rather than identifying the chapter's definitional criterion.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Over-restricts sevā to religious institutions — while langar and prasād are institutional examples, Kabir's grandfather is not, and the chapter presents sevā as a broader social tradition; suggests the student over-relied on the two religious examples.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Overfits to the demographic of the examples given (a retired officer, grandfather) without applying the chapter's definition — suggests the student is pattern-matching to surface features rather than reading the chapter's conceptual claim.
